title: Here is the Fifth Source
paragraphs: > Five characteristics the sources of similitude come to > As one includes things lowly.
Apart from the four sources of simile -- excellence, beauty, love, might -- mentioned earlier, there is a fifth one too.
That is the comparison of the subject with the lowly things.
The Tamil term kiḻakkiṭu poruḷ used in the Tolkāppiyam verse is a trivial thing or something degrading or lowly.

In a big village, a person was working as a washerman assisted by five donkeys. On an eventful night, one of those donkeys was found missing. He went searching for it throughout the night. At the approach of dawn, the washerman thought he heard a donkey bray from a house. “Hurray! I have traced my donkey”, he exulted and entered that house. Actually, it was the singer in the house doing his early morning practice.
The singer was surprised to see this man sprint in, and enquired, “What is the matter?”
He replied, “I have lost my donkey and I am searching for it. Since your music sounded like my donkey’s voice I rushed in here.”
“Now get lost! Stop barking like a dog and get out!” he shouted in rage.
The tempers became frayed which ended up in a big ruckus.
A person from a nearby house approached them and asked, “What men, why are you howling like foxes?”
Now, both these men joined together to take up cudgels against the third person. Fortunately, a grammar teacher who happened to pass by pacified them and explained:

> Making similes using the donkey, dog and fox is an instance of the fifth > basis of simile referred to in the Uvamaiyiyal. This is done to make clear the > inferiority of a particular thing. It is natural to expose its characteristics > through such similes. Hence these are called trivial things.
Though they could not comprehend what he was stating, they could grasp that he was pacifying them through some good advice. They stopped shouting and the quarrel ended.
Thus we see that the sources of a simile come to five when a thing of lowly signification is added.
